title: Paul's letters
tagline: Thirteen letters from a tentmaker turned apostle, written to young churches and trusted friends between his journeys and his prisons.

intro.text: Paul was a Jew of Tarsus in Cilicia, of the tribe of Benjamin, brought up in Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel and trained as a Pharisee. He was a Roman citizen by birth, went by both Saul and Paul, and earned his keep as a tentmaker, working with his own hands.

He first appears as a persecutor of the church. After he met the risen Christ on the road to Damascus he called himself an apostle "not of men", and spent the rest of his life carrying the gospel through Syria, Asia Minor and Greece, and at last, as a prisoner, to Rome.

Thirteen letters in the New Testament carry his name. None of their dates is stated in the Bible: every year on this page is a scholar's reconstruction, and Robertson warned that "there is not a single date in the life of Paul that is beyond dispute". Where the old authorities disagree, their views are set side by side.

author.text: Paul, writing as "a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle". No one shares the opening greeting, but the letter was taken down by a scribe who greets the readers in his own name, Tertius, the only scribe any of Paul's letters names. Seven companions add their greetings at the end.

recipients.text: "All that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints": a church Paul had not yet visited, though he had long meant to, and whose faith was already "spoken of throughout the whole world". No source records how the church at Rome began; Easton thought it likely that visitors from Rome who were in Jerusalem at Pentecost carried the faith home. Acts says the emperor Claudius had ordered all Jews out of Rome, an expulsion the Roman historian Suetonius also records.

writtenFrom.text: Corinth, or its port Cenchrea, by almost every account. Paul commends Phebe of the church at Cenchrea, sends greetings from Gaius, his host (a Gaius of Corinth appears in 1 Corinthians), and from Erastus, the city's chamberlain. Moule (ISBE) names Corinth "with confidence"; Easton and Schaff agree. The old note printed after the letter in the KJV ("from Corinthus") is a later scribal addition, not Scripture, though here it agrees with the usual view.

date.text: Written when Paul had finished preaching "from Jerusalem, and round about unto Illyricum" and was about to carry the collection to Jerusalem, most likely in the three months in Greece of Acts 20. Moule dates it 58, noting that newer schemes move it to 56; Ramsay about January 57; Schaff spring 58; Easton early 58 (though elsewhere he says 55).

occasion.text: Paul was preparing for a visit he had long wanted to make, hoping the church would speed him on to Spain. He asked for prayer for a risky journey to Jerusalem with the gift for its poor, set out the gospel he preached, and spoke to tensions between Jewish and Gentile believers and between the "weak" and the "strong" over food and holy days.

recipients.text: "The church of God which is at Corinth", together with all who call on the name of Jesus Christ in every place. Paul had founded the church on his second journey and stayed eighteen months. Corinth, destroyed by Rome in 146 BC and refounded by Julius Caesar as a colony largely of freedmen, was the capital of the province of Achaia: wealthy, mixed and, in Easton's words, noted for luxury and vice.

writtenFrom.text: Ephesus: "I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost", and "the churches of Asia salute you". The KJV's closing note says "from Philippi"; that note is a later addition, not Scripture, and Easton calls it a mistake, probably a misreading of "I do pass through Macedonia".

date.text: Near the end of Paul's long stay at Ephesus, in a spring before Pentecost. Shaw (ISBE) gives spring 55 or 54, the earlier date leaving room for an extra visit and letter; Ramsay about October 55; Schaff and Easton spring 57.

occasion.text: News reached Paul three ways: a report of quarrels from Chloe's household and of sexual immorality, a letter from the church itself, and a visit from Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus. He had already written them a letter that is now lost. The phrase "Now concerning" opens new subjects six times, and readers often take these as the questions from the Corinthians' letter, though the letter does not say so.

occasion.text: Paul wrote in relief after a crisis: deadly trouble in Asia, then Titus's report that the Corinthians had answered an earlier painful letter with godly sorrow. recipients.text: "The churches of Galatia": several congregations, addressed as "O foolish Galatians", who had first received Paul "as an angel of God" when he came to them in illness. writtenFrom.text: The letter does not say. Proposals include Syrian Antioch (Ramsay), Ephesus ("most interpreters", says Findlay), Macedonia or Corinth (Lightfoot, Easton, Findlay). date.text: The most disputed date of Paul's earlier letters. Calvin placed it before the Council of Jerusalem; Ramsay in AD 53; Schaff 54 to 57; Findlay about 56-57; Lightfoot and Easton 57-58, just before Romans. Which Galatia it was sent to and which Jerusalem visit Galatians 2 describes decide much of the answer.

occasion.text: Teachers had come to Galatia preaching "another gospel", pressing Gentile believers to be circumcised and to keep special days, and undermining Paul's authority. He answers with his own story and an argument from Scripture. Tertullian called it the letter "most decisive against Judaism"; Schaff named its central idea "evangelical freedom".

author.text: Paul, "an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God" and "the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles", with no co-sender, unlike Colossians and Philemon. Since the early nineteenth century some scholars have doubted that Paul wrote it; others have defended it (see the open questions).

recipients.text: "The saints which are at Ephesus, and to the faithful in Christ Jesus", Gentile believers. The words "at Ephesus" are missing from the oldest manuscripts, and the letter sends no personal greetings to a city where Paul had spent about three years, so many have thought it a circular letter for the churches of Asia.

writtenFrom.text: In custody: Paul calls himself a prisoner and "an ambassador in bonds". Traditionally Rome; some nineteenth-century scholars (Böttger, Thiersch, Reuss, Meyer) argued for Caesarea. The Latin prologue in Codex Fuldensis says it was written from prison in Rome and carried by Tychicus. It went out together with Colossians and Philemon, all three carried by Tychicus.

date.text: On the Roman view about 60-63: Lightfoot "about the year 63", Easton about 62, and ISBE about 58 on an early chronology or 63-64 on a later one; on the Caesarean view about 57-59. Which came first, Ephesians or Colossians, is disputed even within Easton's own dictionary.

occasion.text: No crisis is named. Easton saw "no special occasion" and an aim that was "plainly not polemical"; ISBE describes its purpose as setting out God's plan to gather all things into one, with the church as his instrument. Its own prayers ask that the readers know the hope of God's calling, the greatness of his power and the love of Christ that passes knowledge.

author.text: "Paul and Timotheus, the servants of Jesus Christ". Paul writes in the first person throughout and speaks about Timothy, so Timothy joins the greeting rather than the writing. recipients.text: "All the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons", the only greeting of Paul's to name church officers. Philippi was "the chief city of that part of Macedonia, and a colony"; the church began on the second journey with Lydia and a jailer.

writtenFrom.text: In custody, where his bonds were known "in all the palace" and greetings came from "Caesar's household". Most writers, ancient and modern, say Rome; Lightfoot held that "Caesar's household" cannot fairly be made to fit Caesarea, which Paulus, Böttger and Thiersch had proposed. A twentieth-century proposal places it at Ephesus. The Latin prologue in Codex Fuldensis says Rome, with the letter carried by Epaphroditus.

date.text: At Rome either early in the custody, about 61-62 (Lightfoot; Easton), or late, about 63-64, as the last of the prison letters (Hayes in ISBE; Conybeare and Howson); at Caesarea about 57-59. Oeder (1731) stood alone in dating it from Corinth on Paul's first visit.

occasion.text: The Philippians had sent a gift with Epaphroditus, who fell sick almost to death; Paul sends him home with this letter of thanks for support that went back to his days in Thessalonica. He also speaks to rivalry among preachers, a quarrel between two women, and a warning against "the concision".

writtenFrom.text: In bonds, and sent with Ephesians and Philemon by Tychicus. Most of the old sources say Rome; Böttger, Thiersch, Reuss and Meyer argued for Caesarea. The Latin prologue in Codex Fuldensis is the one ancient note that names Ephesus.

date.text: The same as Ephesians and Philemon: about 60-63 on the Roman view (Lightfoot "about the year 63"), about 57-59 on the Caesarean. Easton's "spring of A.D. 57, or, as some think, 62" does not sit easily with his own Roman placing. Lightfoot noted that the letter says nothing of the earthquake that ruined Laodicea, which Tacitus dates to AD 60.

occasion.text: Epaphras brought news, and Paul writes to warn against a teaching built on "philosophy and vain deceit": rules about food, drink, holy days and sabbaths, the "worshipping of angels", visions, and harsh self-denial. What that teaching was is debated: a Jewish mysticism with Essene leanings (Lightfoot), Jewish ideas blended with local Phrygian religion (ISBE), or Eastern mysticism joined to Judaizing (Easton).

recipients.text: "The church of the Thessalonians", in a busy port and market city of Macedonia, governed by its own magistrates, the "rulers of the city" whom Acts calls by their local title, politarchs. Paul founded the church on his second journey, reasoning in the synagogue on three sabbaths; the converts had "turned to God from idols", so the church was largely Gentile.

writtenFrom.text: Corinth, by almost every account: Paul looks back on being "left at Athens alone", and Timothy has just returned from Thessalonica, a reunion Acts places at Corinth. The KJV's closing note, "from Athens", is a later addition, not Scripture; Easton calls it an error.

date.text: Early in Paul's eighteen months at Corinth. Harnack put it as early as 48 and Zahn as late as 53, which Walker (ISBE) takes as the outer limits; Robertson gives 52-53, Schaff 52 or 53, Easton the end of 52, and Ramsay the earlier part of a stay he dates September 51 to March 53. Easton and Milligan count it the first of all Paul's letters, unless Galatians came earlier still.

occasion.text: Forced out after a short stay and hindered from returning, Paul sent Timothy back from Athens and was overjoyed at his report. He writes to defend his conduct against whispered suspicions, to answer questions about believers who had died before the Lord's coming and about "the times and the seasons", and to urge purity and quiet work.

The day of the Lord comes "as a thief in the night".
"Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks".
Spirit, soul and body preserved blameless.

outline.title: Separation, Timothy's mission, and a prayer

words.note: Counted in the Byzantine Greek text: 19 times in 89 verses, the highest rate of Paul's six earlier letters.
The Textus Receptus count is one short because one form at 1 Thess 3:3 is untagged in the site's file.

people.name: Timotheus (Timothy)
people.note: Co-sender; sent back from Athens and returned with good news.

places.name: Greece
places.note: The site's places data tags Greece here; the KJV names Macedonia and Achaia.

otQuotes.note: Allusion: the breastplate and the helmet of salvation. The letter has no formal Old Testament quotation.

author.text: The same three senders as the first letter: "Paul, and Silvanus, and Timotheus". Paul closes with his own signature, "the token in every epistle"; Lightfoot saw such autographs as a guard against forgeries. Whether Paul wrote this letter has been questioned since the nineteenth century (see the open questions).

recipients.text: "The church of the Thessalonians", still under persecution.

writtenFrom.text: Corinth, according to most of the sources, soon after the first letter: Silvanus and Timothy are still with Paul, and the three were together at Corinth, after which Silas drops out of Acts. Easton: "probably also written from Corinth, and not many months after the first". The KJV's closing note, "from Athens", is a later addition, not Scripture.

date.text: For those who hold that Paul wrote it, a little after the first letter: Robertson gives 52-53, following Lightfoot's grouping. Grotius and Ewald, though they accepted both letters, put this one first; Hilgenfeld, who rejected it, dated it to the age of Trajan.

occasion.text: Persecution was continuing; someone was unsettling the church "by spirit, nor by word, nor by letter as from us" with the claim that the day of Christ had already come (a forged letter or a misreading of the first, the verse does not say which); and some had stopped working. Walker calls it "a second prescription for the same case".

themes.text: God's justice for the persecuted.
What must happen before the day of the Lord.
Holding to the apostles' teaching.
The dignity of work, and discipline exercised as among brothers.

keyVerses.why: The Lord revealed from heaven with his mighty angels, in flaming fire.
That day will not come without a falling away first.
"The mystery of iniquity doth already work", held back for now.
"Stand fast, and hold the traditions".
"If any would not work, neither should he eat".
"Be not weary in well doing".
Paul's signature, "the token in every epistle".

author.text: "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God our Saviour", with no co-sender. Since the early nineteenth century many critics have denied that Paul wrote the pastoral letters, while others have defended them (see the open questions).

recipients.text: Timothy, "my own son in the faith", whom Paul had asked to stay on at Ephesus when he went into Macedonia. Timothy was young, of Lystra, with a Jewish mother and a Greek father, and had been set apart by the laying on of the presbytery's hands. The church he served already had elders, deacons and an enrolled list of widows.

writtenFrom.text: Macedonia, on the usual view, after a release from the first Roman custody; Easton suggests Philippi. An ancient subscription and the Codex Fuldensis prologue say Laodicea, which Easton rejects because Paul has just gone on into Macedonia; Lightfoot thought that note grew from guessing that this was the "epistle from Laodicea" of Colossians 4:16.

date.text: On the release view about 63-67: ISBE puts all three pastoral letters within a few years of 64, in the order 1 Timothy, Titus, 2 Timothy, and Easton about 66 or 67. Schaff mentions a proposal to fit it into Paul's Ephesus years (about 56-57); those who deny Paul wrote it place it in the early second century, Baur about 150.

occasion.text: To silence people teaching "other doctrine", "fables and endless genealogies", a misuse of the law, and a ban on marriage and certain foods; Hymenaeus and Alexander had "made shipwreck" of faith. Paul writes so that, if he is delayed, Timothy will know how to behave "in the house of God".

themes.text: Sound teaching against speculative myths and genealogies.
Church order: overseers, deacons, elders and widows.
Godliness, a word used here more than in any other New Testament book.
God the Saviour of all, "who will have all men to be saved".
Money and contentment.
The "faithful sayings": a formula found only in the pastoral letters.

keyVerses.why: The first faithful saying: Christ came to save sinners, "of whom I am chief".
One God, and one mediator between God and men.
The church, "the pillar and ground of the truth".
A six-line confession of "the mystery of godliness". The Textus Receptus reads "God was manifest"; Tischendorf's text reads "who was manifest".
"Let no man despise thy youth".
"Godliness with contentment is great gain".
"The love of money is the root of all evil".
"Fight the good fight of faith".

otQuotes.note: Introduced with "the scripture saith", and paired with a saying that matches Jesus' words in Luke 10:7

author.text: "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God", now a prisoner in Rome who expects to die. Since the early nineteenth century many critics have denied that Paul wrote the pastoral letters, while others have defended them (see the open questions). ISBE argues that personal passages such as the list of who went where are too specific for a forger; Renan thought a later writer had worked in a few genuine notes of Paul's.

recipients.text: Timothy, "my dearly beloved son". Where he was is not stated; Paul greets the household of Onesiphorus and has sent Tychicus to Ephesus, which suggests that region, and asks Timothy to come by way of Troas.

writtenFrom.text: Rome, where Onesiphorus had searched for Paul and found him in chains. Most of the sources, and the Codex Fuldensis prologue, place it in a second Roman imprisonment shortly before Paul's death; those who deny a release place it in the first.

date.text: About 64-67 on the release view; ISBE calls it "the very last of Paul's extant epistles". About 61-62 if Paul was never released; early second century for those who think it the work of a later writer, Pfleiderer placing it in Trajan's reign.

occasion.text: Paul expects death and has been deserted: "all they which are in Asia" have turned away, and at his first hearing no one stood with him. He urges Timothy to be brave, to pass the teaching on, to resist teachers who say the resurrection is already past, and to come quickly, before winter, bringing Mark, the cloak and the parchments.

themes.text: Faithful endurance in suffering.
Guarding and passing on what was committed to him.
The sufficiency of Scripture.
Paul's farewell and his hope of the crown of righteousness.
The Lord's "appearing".

keyVerses.why: Not the spirit of fear, but of power, love and a sound mind.
"I know whom I have believed".
Four generations of teaching: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others.
"Rightly dividing the word of truth".
"All scripture is given by inspiration of God": in Greek, God-breathed.
"Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season".
"I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith".

author.text: "Paul, a servant of God, and an apostle of Jesus Christ". Since the early nineteenth century many critics have denied that Paul wrote the pastoral letters, while others have defended them (see the open questions).

recipients.text: Titus, "mine own son after the common faith", left in Crete to set the churches in order and appoint elders in every city. A Greek whom Jerusalem did not compel to be circumcised, he had been Paul's partner in the dealings with Corinth; Acts never names him.

writtenFrom.text: Not stated. Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis, and the Codex Fuldensis prologue says the letter was written there; the old KJV-era subscription says "Nicopolis of Macedonia", but Easton thinks the city meant is Nicopolis in Epirus, founded by Augustus after Actium.

date.text: Between 1 and 2 Timothy on the release view, about 63-66; Easton puts it "about the same time as the first epistle to Timothy". Those who deny Paul wrote it date it in the second century.

occasion.text: To organise the Cretan churches and to silence "unruly and vain talkers and deceivers", especially those of the circumcision teaching Jewish fables for gain. It closes with travel plans: Artemas or Tychicus will relieve Titus, who is to join Paul at Nicopolis for the winter and to help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way.

themes.text: Sound doctrine that produces good works.
God and Christ both called Saviour, six times, the highest density in the New Testament.
The "appearing" of grace and of Christ.
Self-control for every age and station.

keyVerses.why: The mission: set in order, and ordain elders in every city.
"A prophet of their own" on Cretans; Clement of Alexandria names him as Epimenides.
Grace that brings salvation has appeared; "that blessed hope".
Not by works of righteousness, but by his mercy he saved us.
The last of the five faithful sayings.

author.text: "Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother". Paul writes in the first person, calls himself "Paul the aged", and signs a promise in his own hand. Lightfoot notes that even Marcion left this letter untouched, though some fourth-century readers thought it too slight for an apostle.

recipients.text: Philemon, "our dearly beloved, and fellowlabourer", with Apphia, Archippus "our fellowsoldier" and the church in his house, though the body of the letter speaks to Philemon alone. Lightfoot read the household as father, mother, son and slave, a reconstruction he labels inference.

writtenFrom.text: In bonds, at the same time as Colossians and Ephesians. Rome on the traditional view (Lightfoot, ISBE, Conybeare and Howson, Easton, and the Codex Fuldensis prologue); Caesarea for Böttger, Thiersch, Reuss and Meyer; supporters of an Ephesian imprisonment point to Paul's request for a lodging as easier from a prison nearby.

date.text: With Colossians and Ephesians: about 63 for Lightfoot; about 58 or 63-64 in ISBE; earlier on the Caesarean view.

occasion.text: Onesimus had left Philemon, perhaps owing him something, and became a believer through the imprisoned Paul. Paul sends him back as "a brother beloved", asks Philemon to receive him "as myself", and promises to repay any debt. The letter never says he ran away or stole; those words come from the commentators. How the story ended is not known.

themes.text: Reconciliation.
Brotherhood across social rank: "not now as a servant, but above a servant".
Persuasion by love rather than command.
Partnership.
Deep affection, "bowels" in the KJV, used three times.

keyVerses.why: A prayer that the sharing of faith become effectual.
The hearts of the saints refreshed by Philemon.
"My son Onesimus", once unprofitable, now profitable: a play on his name, which means "useful".
Parted for a season, to be received for ever as a brother beloved.
"Receive him as myself ... put that on mine account ... I will repay it".
Hope of release: "prepare me also a lodging".

questions.question: Who were "the churches of Galatia": the old Celtic territory in the north, or the southern cities of the Roman province?

views.label: North Galatia
views.holders: Earlier scholars up to Lightfoot and Salmon; later Chase, Dods, Sabatier, Harnack, H. Holtzmann, Jülicher, Lipsius, Mommsen, Schmiedel, Schürer and others; Findlay himself (as listed by Findlay, ISBE)

argument.text: The letter went to churches in old Galatia around Ancyra, Pessinus and Tavium, which Paul first reached on his second journey when he passed through "the region of Galatia". On this view the letter is later rather than earlier. Robertson judged in 1915 that it "still has the weight of authority".

views.label: South Galatia
views.holders: First proposed by Mynster (1825); then Perrot, Renan, Pfleiderer, Weizsäcker, Ramsay, von Soden, Bartlet, Gifford, Rendall, Sanday ("with hesitation") and others (as listed by Findlay, ISBE)

argument.text: The letter went to Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, the churches Paul founded on his first journey, all inside the Roman province of Galatia. Ramsay's books made this view widely known from 1895, and some of its supporters make Galatians the earliest of Paul's letters.

questions.question: How many letters did Paul write to Corinth, and which was the letter written "with many tears"?

views.label: Four letters, two of them lost
views.holders: Read from the letters themselves

argument.text: The two surviving letters point to at least four: a lost earlier letter about not keeping company with fornicators, 1 Corinthians, a letter written "out of much affliction and anguish of heart", and 2 Corinthians. Shaw (ISBE) suggests that 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1 may preserve a stray piece of the lost first letter.

views.label: The tearful letter is 1 Corinthians
views.holders: Easton

argument.text: Easton applies Paul's description of anguish and tears to 1 Corinthians itself. He also doubts any unrecorded painful visit, reading "the third time I am ready to come" as an intention only.

views.label: A separate letter, now lost
views.holders: Shaw (ISBE)

argument.text: Shaw treats "the severe letter" as a letter of its own, written after a painful second visit that Acts does not record.

views.label: The tearful letter survives as 2 Corinthians 10-13
views.holders: Hausrath (1870), followed by Schmiedel, Pfleiderer, Lipsius, Clemen, von Soden, McGiffert, Plummer, Moffatt, Peake, J. H. Kennedy and others (as listed by Shaw, ISBE)

argument.text: Everyone agrees on a remarkable change of tone at chapter 10. On this view the last four chapters are part of the painful letter, later joined to the gentler one.

views.label: 2 Corinthians is one letter
views.holders: Sanday, A. Robertson, Holtzmann, Beyschlag, Weizsäcker, Sabatier, Godet, Bernard, Denney, Weiss and Zahn (as listed by Shaw, ISBE)

argument.text: The change of tone is real, but it does not prove that two letters were joined; A. Robertson called the case "decidedly not proven".

questions.question: Was the last chapter of Romans, with its long list of greetings, written to Rome?

views.label: A note to Ephesus attached later
views.holders: Reuss, Ewald and Farrar (named by Schaff); others reported by Moule (ISBE)

argument.text: Paul greets so many people in a city he had never visited that some thought the greetings, Romans 16:1-15 or 16:3-20, belonged to a separate note sent to Ephesus.

views.label: One circular letter with several endings
views.holders: Renan

argument.text: Renan guessed that an editor had combined four copies of a single circular letter, each with a different ending.

views.label: Chapters 15-16 not genuine
views.holders: Baur

argument.text: Baur rejected the last two chapters altogether; Hilgenfeld and Pfleiderer defended them against him.

views.label: Part of the letter to Rome
views.holders: Hort, A. Robertson, Hilgenfeld, Pfleiderer (reported by Moule and Schaff)

argument.text: Of some 300 manuscripts of Romans, Moule reports, not one that is undamaged lacks the complete letter. The doubts in the manuscripts concern the closing doxology, which some copies place after chapter 14 and three, with Marcion, leave out.

questions.question: Did Paul write 2 Thessalonians, and which of the two letters came first?

views.label: Not by Paul
views.holders: Baur (who, Schaff reports, regarded the first letter as an imitation of the second); Hilgenfeld, who dated it to Trajan's reign as "a sort of Pauline Apocalypse" (reported by Schaff)

argument.text: Its teaching on the Lord's coming seems to differ from the first letter ("In the First Letter he coaxes; in the Second Letter he commands", as Walker summarises the case), its tone is cooler, and its "man of sin" is unlike anything else in Paul.

views.label: By Paul
views.holders: Walker (ISBE); Harnack, who thought it was addressed to a Jewish-Christian group in the church

argument.text: Jesus' own teaching holds together "watch, for it may be soon" and "the end is not yet"; and a sterner second note is natural if the gentler first one had not worked. Walker saw scholars of every camp returning to the traditional view.

views.label: Written before 1 Thessalonians
views.holders: Grotius and Ewald, who held both letters genuine (reported by Schaff)

argument.text: The order of the two letters in the Bible is not necessarily the order in which they were written.

questions.question: Where was Paul held when he wrote the prison letters: Rome, Caesarea or Ephesus?

views.label: Rome
views.holders: The oldest tradition and "most modern writers" (Lightfoot); Conybeare and Howson; the ISBE articles; Easton

argument.text: Acts ends with two years in Rome, in a rented house under guard, receiving all who came. Greetings from "Caesar's household" fit Rome; Lightfoot held they could not fairly fit Caesarea, and that at Caesarea, having appealed to Caesar, Paul had no reason to expect release and a visit to Macedonia.

views.label: Caesarea
views.holders: Böttger, Thiersch, Reuss and H. A. W. Meyer for Ephesians, Colossians and Philemon; H. E. G. Paulus, Böttger and Thiersch for Philippians (reported by Lightfoot)

argument.text: Paul was also held two years at Caesarea under Felix, with friends free to visit, and the "palace" of Philippians 1:13 is the same Greek word used for Herod's judgment hall there.

views.label: Ephesus
views.holders: The Latin prologue to Colossians in Codex Fuldensis; modern supporters are twentieth-century scholars not read for this page

argument.text: Paul's own record mentions prisons "more frequent" than Acts reports, a fight with beasts at Ephesus and deadly trouble in Asia, and Clement of Rome says he was in bonds seven times. An Ephesian prison would also explain a request for a lodging at nearby Colossae.

questions.question: Was "Ephesians" written to Ephesus? The words "at Ephesus" are missing from the oldest manuscripts.

views.label: To Ephesus
views.holders: Tertullian, appealing to "the true tradition of the Church"

argument.text: The Textus Receptus and the KJV read "at Ephesus", and the church received the letter under that title.

views.label: To Laodicea
views.holders: Marcion

argument.text: Marcion's collection called it the letter "to the Laodiceans".

views.label: A circular letter for the churches of Asia
views.holders: Archbishop Ussher, who first proposed it; Lightfoot, Conybeare and Howson, Lewis (ISBE), Easton

argument.text: Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus lack "at Ephesus"; Origen knew nothing of the words and Basil reported old copies without them. The letter has no personal greetings, though Paul spent three years at Ephesus, and speaks as if some readers had only heard of him. On this view the copy that reached Laodicea is "the epistle from Laodicea" of Colossians 4:16.

questions.question: Did Paul write Ephesians, Colossians and the pastoral letters?

views.label: All by Paul
views.holders: The ancient church (Eusebius: Paul's letters "well known and undisputed"); for Ephesians and Colossians Bleek, Meyer, B. Weiss, Alford and Farrar; for the pastoral letters Huther, Wiesinger, Wieseler, Lange, Alford, Farrar, Salmon, B. Weiss and others (as listed by Schaff and ISBE)

argument.text: Each letter names Paul in its first verse, and ancient writers accepted all of them. Marcion did reject the pastoral letters, which, Tertullian notes, "all treat of ecclesiastical discipline". Schaff answers the vocabulary argument by noting that Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians and Philippians also have many words found nowhere else in the New Testament.

views.label: Ephesians or Colossians not by Paul
views.holders: De Wette (Ephesians "a verbose expansion" of Colossians); Renan and Ewald (kept Colossians, gave up Ephesians); Mayerhoff (Colossians an abridgment of Ephesians); Baur, Schwegler and Hilgenfeld (both, from a later anti-Gnostic writer); Holtzmann, Pfleiderer and others

argument.text: The two letters overlap so closely that critics have argued one is a later writer's reworking of the other, or both of something earlier. ISBE concludes instead for "simultaneous authorship by one writer".

views.label: The pastoral letters not by Paul
views.holders: J. E. C. Schmidt and Schleiermacher (1 Timothy); Baur, who dated them about 150; Holtzmann, whose 1880 work made the fullest case from their vocabulary; Renan, Pfleiderer, Ewald, Hausrath and others

argument.text: Holtzmann made the fullest case from their language: Schaff, citing him, counts 169 of their words found nowhere else in the New Testament. Baur dated them about 150, and Pfleiderer placed 2 Timothy under Trajan and the other two under Hadrian. Renan thought a forger had worked in a few genuine notes of Paul's.

questions.question: Was Paul released after the two years in Rome, and imprisoned a second time?

views.label: Released, travelled, arrested again and executed
views.holders: Eusebius; Conybeare and Howson, adding Chrysostom and Jerome; ISBE; Easton; Schaff ("disposed to admit" it)

argument.text: The pastoral letters mention journeys that do not fit Acts: Timothy left at Ephesus, Titus in Crete, a winter at Nicopolis, a cloak at Troas. Clement of Rome says Paul reached "the farthest bounds of the West"; the Muratorian fragment speaks of a journey from Rome to Spain; and Eusebius reports that Paul was sent out again to preach and martyred on a second visit to Rome, citing 2 Timothy's "first answer".

views.label: Not released
views.holders: Wieseler and Schrader (as criticised by Conybeare and Howson)

argument.text: Acts and the other early sources are silent about later travel, and Clement's "farthest bounds of the West" may simply mean Rome.

views.label: Pastoral letters written during the Acts period
views.holders: One proposal reported by Schaff

argument.text: The journeys could be unrecorded trips during Paul's three years at Ephesus, about 56-57.

views.label: No evidence either way
views.holders: Those who deny that Paul wrote the pastoral letters

argument.text: If the pastoral letters are not Paul's, their travel notes say nothing about his last years.

claim.text: Writing to Corinth about AD 95, Clement tells them to "take up the epistle of the blessed Paul", recalling the parties named after Paul, Cephas and Apollos: one of the earliest references to a letter of Paul outside the New Testament. Moule says he repeatedly quotes Romans; echoes of Ephesians, Philippians and 2 Timothy are noted by ISBE, Lightfoot and Schaff. He is silent about 2 Corinthians where he might have used it.

Ignatius (about 107-110) echoes 1 Corinthians ("Where is the wise? Where is the disputer?"), and is said to quote Romans and echo Galatians and Philippians. He tells the Ephesians that Paul mentions them "in all his Epistles", and ISBE notes he plays on the name Onesimus.

Polycarp (first half of the second century) echoes Romans, 2 Corinthians, Galatians and 2 Thessalonians, cites "the saints shall judge the world, as Paul teacheth", quotes Ephesians 4:26 as "these Scriptures", quotes 1 Timothy on the love of money, uses 2 Timothy's "loved ... this present world", and reminds the Philippians that Paul wrote to them.

About 140 Marcion gathered ten letters in this order: Galatians, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Romans, 1 and 2 Thessalonians, "Laodiceans" (Ephesians), Colossians, Philippians, Philemon. Tertullian's reply follows that order, says Philemon's brevity alone saved it from Marcion's editing, and reports that he rejected the two letters to Timothy and the one to Titus. Lightfoot doubted that Marcion's order was meant to be chronological.

Irenaeus (about 180) quotes Paul's letters by name: "the Epistle to the Romans", "the Second to the Corinthians", "the Epistle to the Galatians", "the first Epistle to the Thessalonians", "the Epistle to the Ephesians". He opens Against Heresies with 1 Timothy's "vain genealogies" and identifies the Linus of 2 Timothy with the first bishop of Rome.

claim.text: The Muratorian fragment says Paul wrote to seven churches by name, twice to the Corinthians and Thessalonians, and also one letter to Philemon, one to Titus and two to Timothy, "hallowed in the esteem of the Catholic Church". It rejects a letter "to the Laodiceans" then in circulation as forged.
Clement of Alexandria (about 200) uses Ephesians, Philippians and Colossians, and quotes Titus 1:12, naming the Cretan prophet as Epimenides.

Answering Marcion letter by letter, Tertullian calls Galatians "the most decisive against Judaism", insists on "the true tradition of the Church" that Ephesians was sent to Ephesus, and defends the letters to Timothy and Titus that Marcion had rejected.

"Paul's fourteen epistles are well known and undisputed," wrote Eusebius about 325; his fourteen include Hebrews, which he notes some rejected. He also records the traditions that Timothy was first bishop of Ephesus and Titus of the churches of Crete.

flows.title: Where Paul's Old Testament quotations come from

claim.text: Each band joins an Old Testament book to a letter that quotes it; its width is the number of places in the letter that quote that book (a passage drawing on two verses of one book counts once). Allusions are left out. The lists are the dossiers' selection of clear quotations, not a census of every echo. Romans quotes far more than any other letter, above all from Isaiah and the Psalms; Habakkuk 2:4, Genesis 15:6, Leviticus 18:5 and Leviticus 19:18 are quoted in both Romans and Galatians.
Lightfoot's first group, in a grouping Robertson (ISBE) still thought the best: the two letters to Thessalonica, written from Corinth during the stay of Acts 18, about 52-53.

Lightfoot's second group, about 55-58: "the great doctrinal group" (Robertson), turning on the dispute over the Jewish law. German scholars call them the chief letters (Hauptbriefe); Ramsay "the four great letters", Schaff "the four great Epistles". Some who hold the South Galatia view would move Galatians earlier.

Lightfoot's third group, about 61-63, which Robertson places in the first Roman imprisonment; Schaff heads them "The Epistles of the Captivity". Each says Paul is in bonds. Some scholars put one or more of them at Caesarea.

Lightfoot's fourth group, after the events of Acts: so called, says ISBE, "because they were addressed to two Christian ministers". Robertson wrote that they are "still hotly disputed"; Schaff held only that 2 Timothy is Paul's farewell.
